17470: A windowsill is the flat, horizontal ledge at the very bottom of a window. Think of it as a narrow shelf that is built right into the base of a window opening. It runs the full width of the window, left to right.

Picture a window on a wall. The window has a frame around it — a border of wood, metal, or plastic that holds the glass in place. Now look at the very bottom edge of that frame. The flat, outward-sticking surface right there — the part that is roughly at the level of the glass's lowest edge — is the windowsill.

It sits where the window meets the wall below it.

A windowsill is a flat, usually rectangular surface. It is wider than the wall is thick, so it sticks out a little — both into the room on the inside, and outward from the building on the outside. It is not a deep surface; it is more like a wide ledge than a table. Its depth (front to back) is usually just a few centimetres to about 15–25 centimetres, depending on the thickness of the wall and the design of the window.

Every window actually has two windowsills:

  • The interior windowsill — this is the one inside your room, on the inside of the wall. It faces upward into the room. This is the one people most commonly refer to in everyday speech when they say "windowsill."
  • The exterior windowsill (sometimes called the window ledge) — this is the one on the outside of the building. It faces outward and slightly downward, and is specifically shaped to allow rainwater to run off instead of soaking into the wall. This outer one is sometimes just called the "window ledge" to distinguish it from the inner one, though the two terms overlap in casual use.

In everyday conversation, when someone says "windowsill" without any extra explanation, they almost always mean the interior one — the flat ledge inside the room.

The material depends on the window and the building:

  • Wood — the most traditional and common material, especially in older homes.
  • Stone or marble — found in older, grander buildings; very durable and attractive.
  • PVC or vinyl — common in modern homes; easy to clean and resistant to moisture.
  • Concrete or brick — often seen in industrial-style buildings or on exterior sills.
  • Tile — sometimes used on interior sills in kitchens or bathrooms.

The windowsill serves both a practical and a decorative purpose.

Practically:

  • On the exterior, it channels rainwater away from the wall, protecting the building from water damage.
  • On the interior, it closes the gap between the window frame and the inner wall, giving the window a neat, finished appearance.

In everyday life, people use the interior windowsill to:

  • Place potted plants, since the sill gets natural sunlight from the window.
  • Display decorative objects like candles, small sculptures, or framed photos.
  • Rest small items temporarily — a book, a cup of tea, your phone.
  • Sit and lean against while looking outside, especially in bay windows where the sill can be wide enough to sit on.
  • In older homes, people sometimes kept perishable food cool on the outer sill before refrigerators were common.

These two terms are often used interchangeably, and in casual conversation that is perfectly fine. However, if you want to be precise:

  • Windowsill most naturally refers to the flat ledge inside the room, at the base of the window.
  • Window ledge can refer to either the inside or outside ledge, but is used especially for the exterior one — the protruding stone or concrete shelf visible from outside the building.

In practice, most people use both terms loosely and are understood without confusion.

• She placed a small cactus on the windowsill where it could get enough sunlight.
  • The cat curled up on the windowsill and watched the street below.
  • He rested his arms on the windowsill and gazed out at the rain.
  • The paint on the old wooden windowsill had started to peel and crack.
  • Pigeons often land on the exterior windowsill of their apartment.

A windowsill is the flat, shelf-like ledge built into the bottom of a window. Inside a room, it is the surface people place plants and objects on and lean against. Outside a building, it is the protruding ledge that keeps water from running down the wall. It is a simple but essential part of any window's structure and plays both a functional and a decorative role in architecture and home life.
17471: Windswept describes something that has been exposed to strong, persistent wind — and shows it. The word is built from two ideas: wind (moving air) and swept (the past tense of "sweep," meaning to pass over a surface forcefully and continuously). So when you call something windswept, you are saying that the wind has swept over it — powerfully, repeatedly, and noticeably.
The two main ways it is used

1. Describing places and landscapes

This is the most common and most powerful use. A windswept place is one that is open, exposed, and battered by the wind. There are no natural shelters — no tall buildings, dense forests, or mountains to block the wind. The wind arrives freely and with full force.

Think of:

  • A bare clifftop above the sea
  • A treeless highland moor
  • An open beach in winter
  • A mountain summit
  • A remote prairie

These places feel raw and wild. When you stand in a windswept location, you feel the wind as a constant presence — it pushes against you, rushes past your ears, and dominates the environment. The word often implies a kind of dramatic, elemental power. Nature is in charge there.

"She stood on the windswept hillside, looking out over the grey sea."

"The windswept coastline was beautiful but brutal in winter."

2. Describing the appearance of things shaped or tossed by wind

Here, windswept describes how something looks after the wind has acted on it — either over a long time (permanently shaping it) or in the recent moment (temporarily messing it up).

Trees and vegetation: A windswept tree is one that the wind has permanently bent and shaped. If strong winds blow from one direction year after year, a tree's trunk leans away from the wind, and its branches all grow to one side, as if being blown even when the air is still. The tree has been sculpted by the wind. This is one of the most vivid and classic uses of the word.

"A lone windswept pine clung to the edge of the cliff."

Hair: Windswept hair is hair that the wind has blown around — tousled, disheveled, out of place. It looks the way hair looks when you have been out in strong wind: loosened from its style, slightly wild, blown across the face.

"He arrived at the door with a red nose and windswept hair."

This use can sometimes carry a slightly attractive, fresh, or adventurous quality — the look of someone who has just come in from the outdoors. But it can also simply mean messy and untidy, depending on context.

Clothing and objects: Less commonly, things like coats, flags, or sand dunes can be called windswept when they have been visibly pushed, shaped, or scattered by wind.
The feeling and atmosphere the word carries

Words carry not just meaning but also a mood — and windswept is a particularly atmospheric word. It almost always brings a sense of:

  • Wildness and rawness: There is something untamed about a windswept place. It has not been softened or controlled. Nature is present and strong.
  • Openness and exposure: A windswept place is never enclosed or sheltered. Everything is out in the open, under the sky.
  • Remoteness or solitude: Windswept places tend to be far from cities and crowds. They feel lonely, sometimes desolate, but often in a way that is more grand than sad.
  • Drama and beauty: Writers and poets use windswept to evoke romantic, dramatic landscapes — the Scottish Highlands, the Irish coast, the American Great Plains, the Patagonian steppe. The word has a literary, almost cinematic quality.

Because of this, windswept is not a neutral word. It does not merely state a fact about wind; it paints a picture and sets a mood.
When the word has a slightly negative tone

While windswept is often used admiringly, it can sometimes carry a note of bleakness or discomfort. A windswept wasteland, a windswept winter street, or a windswept industrial estate does not sound appealing — it sounds cold, bare, and harsh. The word then suggests a place that is unpleasantly exposed and lacking any warmth or protection.

So the emotional tone of windswept depends on what it is describing. Applied to a dramatic coastline or rugged highland, it feels magnificent. Applied to a flat car park or a bleak town square, it can sound dreary.

To use the word confidently, remember this: windswept means visibly shaped by, exposed to, or tossed by strong wind. It describes a place that the wind rules over, a tree or landscape permanently marked by the wind's force, or hair and appearance made messy or wild by the wind. It almost always carries a feeling of wildness, openness, and natural power — and whether that feels beautiful or bleak depends on what is being described.

If you picture someone standing on a rugged sea cliff, hair blowing back, the cold wind roaring in off the ocean, the grass flattening around them, and one lone tree nearby bent permanently sideways — that entire scene, every part of it, could be called windswept.
17472:
To "wing it" means to do something without any preparation, planning, or practice — you just figure it out as you go, relying on your natural ability, instinct, or quick thinking in the moment.

When you wing it, you haven't rehearsed, you haven't studied, you haven't made a plan. You simply jump into the situation and handle it on the spot.
A Simple Way to Picture It

Imagine a bird learning to fly. It doesn't read a manual. It doesn't take a class. It simply spreads its wings and tries — figuring out what to do as it's already doing it. That's the spirit of "winging it."
Where Did This Idiom Come From?

The expression comes from the world of theatre, dating back to the 1800s.

In old theatres, the areas just off the sides of the stage — hidden from the audience — were called "the wings." When an actor hadn't fully memorized their lines or didn't have enough time to prepare, a prompter would stand in the wings and whisper the lines to the actor during the actual live performance.

So the actor was essentially performing from the wings — getting help at the last second, improvising, and muddling through without being fully ready.

Over time, the phrase expanded beyond theatre and into everyday life. Today it simply means doing anything without proper preparation.

Here are some natural, real-world examples:

Example 1 — A speech:

"I forgot to prepare my presentation, so I just winged it in front of the whole class."

→ The person had no notes, no practice — they spoke off the top of their head.

Example 2 — Cooking:

"I didn't follow any recipe. I just winged it and threw whatever vegetables I found into the pan."

→ No plan, no recipe — just improvising in the kitchen.

Example 3 — A job interview:

"She didn't research the company at all. She completely winged the interview."

→ She went in unprepared and hoped things would go well anyway.

Example 4 — A conversation:

"I don't know anything about cricket, but if they bring it up at the party, I'll just wing it."

→ He'll pretend to know, or figure out something to say on the spot.

Example 5 — A test:

"I never studied for the exam. I just winged it and hoped for the best."
The Tone: Is It Positive or Negative?

This is an important nuance. The tone depends entirely on context and outcome.

Casual / Lighthearted (Neutral or Positive):
Sometimes "winging it" is seen as fun, brave, or impressively skillful. If someone wings a speech and delivers it brilliantly, people admire their confidence and natural talent.

"He winged the whole stand-up comedy routine and the audience loved it!"

Negative / Irresponsible:
In serious or professional situations — surgery, law, engineering, a crucial business meeting — winging it is seen as careless or reckless.

"You can't just wing it when lives are at stake."

So the idiom itself is neutral, but the judgment around it shifts based on what's being winged and how it turns out.

The idiom changes form based on grammar, just like a regular verb:

SituationForm
Right now"I'm winging it."
Past"I winged it."
Future / plan"I'll just wing it."
General habit"She always wings it."
Noun form"It was a total wing-it situation."

More naturally:

  • "I'm winging it" — present, happening now
  • "I winged it" — past tense
  • "I'll wing it" — future
  • "wing-it approach / wing-it strategy" — used as an adjective to describe a style of doing things

These all carry a similar meaning:

  • "Go with the flow" — be flexible, adapt as things happen (slightly softer)
  • "Improvise" — make it up as you go (more formal/neutral)
  • "Fly by the seat of your pants" — another vivid idiom meaning to manage a situation using instinct, with no preparation (more emphasis on the difficulty)
  • "Play it by ear" — decide what to do based on the situation as it unfolds (often used for plans that are deliberately kept flexible, not necessarily unplanned)
  • "Ad-lib" — speak or perform without a script (mostly used in acting/speaking contexts)

Key difference: "Wing it" always implies a lack of preparation specifically. "Play it by ear" can mean you're intentionally leaving things open-ended, not necessarily that you were unprepared.

To avoid confusion:

  • It does not mean doing something with your arms or physically flying.
  • It does not mean doing something badly — you can wing it and still do well.
  • It does not mean giving up — you're still genuinely trying, just without preparation.
  • It is not the same as being lazy. Sometimes you wing it because circumstances forced you to (no time, unexpected situation), not because you chose not to prepare.

Whenever you hear "wing it," picture a bird jumping off a branch for the first time — no coaching, no runway, no plan. Just spreading its wings and figuring out flight in mid-air.

That image captures the idiom perfectly: acting in the moment, without preparation, trusting yourself to figure it out as you go.
"Wing it" = Do something without preparation, figuring it out as you go.
17473: "Winning" as an adjective has two distinct meanings. You need to know both to fully own this word.
Meaning 1 — The one that succeeded or achieved victory

In any competition, contest, game, or race, many people or things compete, but only one comes out on top. "Winning" is the word that points to that one — the team, the goal, the ticket, the move — that achieved success.

Think of it as a label that says: this is the one that won.

  • The winning team received the trophy. → The team that won.
  • She scored the winning goal in the final minute. → The goal that secured the victory.
  • He held the winning lottery ticket. → The ticket that turned out to be the lucky one.
  • Their winning strategy was to stay patient and attack late. → The strategy that led to their victory.

Notice that "winning" here is purely factual and objective. It doesn't say anything emotional — it simply identifies which one came out on top. Either something won, or it didn't. "The winning bid" at an auction is simply the highest bid that beat all others. "A winning formula" is a method that has been proven to work, especially one that works repeatedly — for example: After years of struggle, the team finally found their winning formula.
Meaning 2 — Naturally charming and attractive in a way that draws people in

This is the subtler, more interesting meaning — and the one that surprises most learners.

Here, "winning" describes a personal quality — usually a smile, a personality, or a general manner — that is so naturally warm, genuine, and appealing that people feel drawn to you almost immediately and instinctively.

The key idea is effortlessness and genuineness. A "winning smile" isn't simply a nice smile. It's one that feels completely natural and authentic — the kind that makes people instantly like you, trust you, and feel good in your presence. It doesn't feel performed or forced. Similarly, a "winning personality" isn't just a pleasant one — it's one that captures people's affection seemingly without trying.

  • She walked into the room with a winning smile. → Her smile was so genuinely warm and charming that it immediately won people over.
  • His winning personality made everyone love him at once. → His natural charm drew people to him effortlessly.
  • Despite being new to the company, her winning ways quickly earned her the respect of her colleagues. → Her natural warmth and charm made people like and trust her fast.
  • The young politician won over the crowd with his winning manner. → The way he carried and expressed himself was so likable that the crowd was immediately on his side.

"Winning ways" is a very common phrase worth remembering. It means the natural habits, behaviors, or qualities of a person that make others like them — their natural charm in action.
How to tell the two meanings apart

Context makes it clear every time. Ask yourself: Is this about a competition or a contest? Then it's Meaning 1. Is this about charm, personality, or social appeal? Then it's Meaning 2.

  • "The winning entry in the photography contest" → Meaning 1 (it won the contest).
  • "A winning smile" → Meaning 2 (naturally charming and attractive).
How to tell when "winning" is an adjective versus a verb

This is an important distinction because "winning" can also appear as part of a verb.

When it's an adjective, it sits directly before a noun and describes it — it answers "what kind of?" or "which one?"
→ "the winning team," "a winning smile," "the winning goal"

When it's a verb (specifically a present participle), it describes an action happening in time.
→ "She is winning the race." / "They kept winning every match."

A simple test: if you can replace "winning" with another descriptive word — like victorious (for Meaning 1) or charming (for Meaning 2) — and the sentence still makes sense structurally, then it's an adjective.

  • "The victorious team received the trophy." ✓ → adjective.
  • "She is victorious the race." ✗ → this doesn't work, so "winning" there is a verb.
The overall feel and tone of the word

Both meanings of "winning" are always positive. Whether something wins a competition or someone wins people's hearts, "winning" describes something successful, favorable, or appealing. It carries no negative or neutral shade.

One final note on Meaning 2 specifically: it is a slightly formal or literary word. You're more likely to encounter it in books, journalism, or careful speech than in casual everyday conversation. But it fits beautifully in writing and adds a touch of elegance when used well.
17474:
To winnow means to carefully separate what is valuable or good from what is worthless or unwanted — and then discard the unwanted part, keeping only what matters.

Think of it as a filtering process driven by judgment. You start with a large, mixed collection of things. You apply careful thought or a smart method. You end up with a smaller, purer, higher-quality result.
The Literal Picture (helps understand the word deeply)

The word originally described what farmers did with harvested grain.

After cutting wheat, the grain comes mixed with chaff — the dry, papery husks that wrap around each grain. Chaff is useless; you can't eat it. But grain is precious. So farmers would toss the mix up into the air. The breeze would carry away the light, worthless chaff, while the heavier grain fell back down into the basket. What remained was pure, clean grain — ready to use.

That act of tossing grain into the wind to separate the good from the bad — that was winnowing.
The Figurative Meaning (how it's actually used today)

Today, people use "winnow" far beyond farming. The idea stays exactly the same: remove the bad to reveal the good. It always involves:

  • Starting with a large, messy, or mixed group
  • Applying careful thought, criteria, or judgment
  • Reducing it to a smaller, cleaner, more worthy set

Some real examples:

"The hiring manager winnowed 500 applications down to 12 for interviews."

She didn't randomly discard applications. She read carefully, applied standards, and eliminated the weaker ones — just like wind blows away chaff.

"The editor winnowed the rough draft, cutting chapters that added nothing to the story."

The bad writing was removed; the good writing remained.

"After years of testing, scientists winnowed the data to find only the patterns that were truly significant."

Noise removed. Signal kept.

"Life eventually winnows your friendships — the casual acquaintances fall away, and the real ones remain."

Time acts as the filter here.

Winnow down — used when reducing a large group to a smaller one:

"We need to winnow down the list of venues to just three options."

Winnow out — used when removing specific unwanted elements:

"Good questioning helps winnow out weak arguments from strong ones."

Winnow through — used when carefully sorting through a large volume of material:

"She spent the afternoon winnowing through hundreds of emails to find the important ones."
What Makes Winnowing Different from Just "Removing" Things

This is important. You could say "he removed some candidates." That's neutral — maybe he removed randomly, maybe by mistake.

But "he winnowed the candidates" tells you three things at once:

  1. He started with many and ended with fewer.
  2. He used judgment and discernment to do it — not chance.
  3. What remained is the better portion — the grain, not the chaff.

Winnowing always implies intelligence and purpose behind the removal. The person (or process) doing the winnowing knows what's good and what isn't, and acts accordingly.

"Winnow" carries a sense of patience and refinement. It's not a violent or hasty action. It suggests careful, methodical separation — the way a skilled editor reads every sentence, or the way a good mentor recognizes which habits a student should keep and which should go.

It's a word used when the quality of what remains matters deeply.

If you can answer yes to all three of these, "winnow" fits perfectly:

  1. Did you start with more and end with less?
  2. Was the reduction based on judgment or a meaningful standard?
  3. Is what remains genuinely better or more useful than what was discarded?

If yes — that's winnowing.
17475: Winsome describes a person who has a sweet, gentle, and naturally appealing charm — the kind that makes people feel instantly warm and drawn toward them. It is charm that feels innocent, fresh, and effortless. Nobody had to try to make you like them; you just did, almost automatically.
Unpacking the feeling of the word

Think of someone — perhaps a child, a young person, or even an adult — whose smile is so open and genuine that it melts the room. Or someone whose personality is so pleasant, light, and sincere that people around them simply feel good. That quality — that soft, likeable radiance — is what "winsome" captures.

The key texture of the word is innocence combined with appeal. It is not the dramatic, powerful attractiveness of someone who commands a room. It is quieter than that. It is the charm of someone who is simply, naturally delightful to be around, without any showiness or performance behind it.

This is important for a learner, because winsome is often confused with similar words.

  • Beautiful is about physical looks alone. A person can be beautiful but cold or off-putting. Winsome goes beyond looks — it includes personality and manner.
  • Charming can sometimes feel calculated or even slick — charm can be used deliberately to win people over, and it can have a slightly manipulative edge. Winsome never does. It is always sincere and unaffected.
  • Cute is casual and can apply to almost anything — a puppy, a mug, a joke. Winsome is more specific: it describes a genuinely appealing human quality.
  • Attractive is a broad, general word. Winsome is more precise — it points to a particular kind of attraction: gentle, sweet, and warm.
  • Charismatic suggests strong, magnetic energy that draws crowds. Winsome is softer and more personal — it works on an individual level, not a stage.

So: winsome sits in its own lane — sweet, unforced, innocent, and genuinely pleasing.

Winsome most commonly describes:

  • A person — "She was a winsome young woman whom everyone seemed to adore."
  • A smile — "He gave the committee a winsome smile, and the tension in the room dissolved."
  • A manner or personality — "There was something winsome about the way he spoke — so earnest and warm."
  • An expression — "The child looked up with a winsome expression that no one could resist."

It does not typically describe objects, landscapes, or abstract ideas. It is almost exclusively a word about human appeal — the way a person looks, smiles, behaves, or carries themselves.
Strength and tone of the word

Winsome is a moderate word in terms of intensity. It does not suggest breathtaking or overwhelming beauty. It suggests something quieter: a steady, pleasant, likeable quality that endears a person to others. Think of it as warmth turned into charm.

It is always a positive word. There is no negative or sarcastic use of winsome. When someone is called winsome, it is a genuine, soft compliment.

It also carries a slightly formal or literary tone. You will encounter it more in novels, formal writing, or careful speech than in everyday casual conversation. If you use it in a text message, it will sound sophisticated. In a piece of writing or a thoughtful conversation, it will sound perfectly natural.

"The new teacher had a winsome personality that made even difficult students eager to come to class."
→ She wasn't stern, flashy, or overpowering — she was naturally warm and appealing, and that drew people in.

"He flashed a winsome grin and somehow convinced the shopkeeper to give him a discount."
→ His smile was so sweet and genuine that it was hard to say no to him.

"There was something undeniably winsome about the way she laughed — light, honest, and completely free."
→ Her laughter had that pure, natural quality that made her immediately likeable.
If you ever need to recall this word quickly: winsome = sweetly and innocently charming in a way that feels effortless and genuine, making others feel naturally drawn to a person.
17476:
Wintry means having the qualities, feel, or appearance of winter — or, by extension, anything that resembles what winter feels like, even if it has nothing to do with actual weather.

That's the seed of the word. Everything else grows from there.
The Literal Meaning: Describing Weather and Nature

In its most direct use, wintry describes weather, landscapes, or conditions that look or feel like winter:

  • Bitter cold
  • Grey, overcast skies
  • Ice, frost, or snow
  • A sense of bleakness, emptiness, or harshness in the environment

Notice that wintry is richer than just saying "cold." Cold tells you the temperature. Wintry paints a whole picture — the sky is grey and low, the trees are bare, the wind has a bite to it, and there's a kind of raw, stripped-down quality to the world.

Examples:

  • "A wintry blast swept across the open fields."
  • "The forecast warned of wintry conditions on the mountain roads."
  • "She looked out at the wintry landscape — grey, bare, and silent."

A wintry mix, a phrase common in weather forecasts, means a combination of snow, sleet, and freezing rain — all those unpleasant frozen things winter throws at you at once.
The Figurative Meaning: Describing People and Emotions

This is where wintry becomes especially powerful and interesting.

Because winter is associated with coldness, bleakness, and a kind of emotional austerity, the word is very commonly used to describe human behaviour, expressions, and feelings that mirror those qualities.

Think about what winter feels like emotionally — not just physically:

  • Unfriendly
  • Unwelcoming
  • Cheerless
  • Lacking warmth or affection
  • Distant, cold, or harsh

When you apply that to a person or their behaviour, you get the figurative meaning of wintry.

Examples:

  • "She gave him a wintry smile."
    → This smile is technically a smile, but it's cold, barely there, and carries no real warmth. It's the kind of smile that doesn't reach the eyes — polite on the surface, but chilly underneath.
  • "The manager received the new idea with a wintry silence."
    → Not just silence, but a cold, unwelcoming silence — the kind that tells you the idea isn't going anywhere.
  • "His tone was wintry and distant."
    → He wasn't shouting or being cruel, but his manner was cold, stiff, and emotionally remote.
  • "She was met with a wintry reception."
    → She was not welcomed warmly. The atmosphere was cold and unfriendly.

This figurative use is very common in literature, journalism, and everyday sophisticated writing. When a writer says someone has a "wintry expression," they mean the face is cold, closed off, and offering nothing warm.

What makes wintry more precise than simply saying "cold" or "unfriendly" is that it carries with it a sense of bleakness and desolation — not just an absence of warmth, but an atmosphere that is grey, stripped down, and somewhat harsh.

Compare these:

  • "He gave me a cold look." — straightforward, describes the temperature of his manner.
  • "He gave me a wintry look." — this is more vivid. You can almost feel the grey sky behind it. There's something bleak and unwelcoming about it, like standing outside in January wind.

Wintry carries a slight literary and atmospheric quality that plain "cold" does not. It's chosen when a writer wants to evoke not just emotional temperature, but also a kind of bleakness or emptiness.
One More Shade: Age and Decline

In literary and poetic writing, wintry is sometimes used to suggest old age, the late stage of life, or the decline of something. This comes from the metaphor of human life as seasons: spring = youth, summer = prime, autumn = middle age, winter = old age or the end.

  • "His wintry years were spent in quiet solitude."
    → The final years of his life.
  • "The kingdom had entered a wintry period of decline."
    → A cold, bleak, fading era.

This use is less common in everyday speech but fairly standard in literature and formal writing.

ContextWhat "wintry" describes

To put it simply:

  1. Weather/nature → cold, grey, bleak, icy, characteristic of winter
  2. Human expression/manner → cold, unfriendly, unwelcoming, emotionally distant
  3. Literary/poetic → associated with the end of life, decline, bleakness

These are words that naturally appear alongside wintry. Knowing them helps you recognize and use the word confidently:

  • Wintry weather — cold, harsh weather typical of winter
  • Wintry conditions — dangerous or difficult conditions caused by ice, snow, cold
  • Wintry mix — a weather forecast term for snow + sleet + freezing rain together
  • Wintry smile — a cold, emotionless, or barely warm smile
  • Wintry look / stare / gaze — an expression that is cold and unwelcoming
  • Wintry silence — a cold, uncomfortable, unwelcoming silence
  • Wintry reception — an unfriendly welcome
  • Wintry landscape / scene — a view that is grey, bare, frozen, and bleak
  • Wintry blast — a sudden rush of cold wind
  • Wintry sky — a grey, heavy, overcast sky

If you want to truly feel the word rather than just define it:

Imagine stepping outside on a January morning. The sky is an unbroken sheet of grey. The trees are bare. The wind cuts into your face. Everything feels a little raw, a little harsh, a little emptied out. The world isn't hostile exactly, but it offers you no comfort. It's cold — not just in temperature, but in mood.

That feeling — that cold, bleak, bare, inhospitable quality — is what wintry means, whether you're talking about the weather outside or the look on someone's face.

Wintry is a slightly formal and literary word. You'll see it more in:

  • Written English (news, literature, formal essays)
  • Weather forecasts (especially in British English)
  • Descriptive writing

In casual conversation, people more often just say "cold" or "freezing" for weather, and "unfriendly" or "icy" for people. But wintry is not uncommon — it's just more deliberate and evocative when it appears.
17477: Before diving into the different uses, understand the heart of this phrase: "wipe out" means to remove something so completely that almost nothing is left. Think of wiping a whiteboard clean — you don't just reduce what's there, you erase it entirely. That feeling of total removal runs through every use of this phrase.

1. To completely destroy or eliminate something

This is the most common and important meaning. When something is "wiped out," it is destroyed so thoroughly that it practically ceases to exist.

Examples:

  • "The flood wiped out the entire village." (The village was completely destroyed.)
  • "The disease wiped out half the population." (Half the people were killed.)
  • "The new app wiped out the competition." (Competing businesses were completely crushed and driven out of the market.)
  • "The fire wiped out years of research." (All that work was lost forever.)

Notice how in each case, the destruction is total, not partial. You wouldn't say "wiped out" if only some damage was done.

2. To exhaust someone completely

In everyday informal speech, "wipe out" is used to describe a person being completely drained of energy — physically or mentally. Here, it is usually used in the passive form: someone is "wiped out."

Examples:

  • "I'm completely wiped out after that 12-hour shift."
  • "The hike wiped me out — I slept for ten hours."
  • "She felt totally wiped out after the exams."

The logic connects to the core idea: your energy has been removed entirely, leaving you empty. This meaning is very informal and common in spoken English.

3. To fall or crash badly (especially in sports)

In sports like surfing, skateboarding, skiing, and cycling, "wipe out" means to fall suddenly and badly, usually losing complete control.

Examples:

  • "He wiped out on a massive wave and lost his board."
  • "She wiped out going around the sharp bend on her bike."
  • "The skier wiped out near the finish line."

This meaning is vivid — it paints the picture of someone being knocked flat, like being swept off their feet. It is casual and common among sports enthusiasts.

4. To destroy someone financially

When money, savings, or wealth is completely lost, "wipe out" is used.

Examples:

  • "The stock market crash wiped out his entire savings."
  • "The lawsuit wiped out the company's profits for the year."
  • "One bad investment wiped her out financially."

Again, the idea of total loss is key here. It's not just losing some money — it's losing everything or nearly everything.

5. To kill someone (informal, often in crime contexts)

In informal or slang contexts — particularly in crime stories, movies, or street language — "wipe out" can mean to kill someone.

Examples:

  • "The hitman was hired to wipe out the witness."
  • "The gang tried to wipe out their rivals."

This usage is more dramatic and tends to appear in fiction, films, or casual storytelling rather than serious or formal writing.

When you turn this phrase into a noun, you write it as one word: wipeout (or sometimes "wipe-out"). It refers to the event of being wiped out.

Examples:

  • "The business suffered a total wipeout during the recession." (Complete financial destruction.)
  • "That was an epic wipeout on the skateboard ramp!" (A spectacular crash.)
  • "The team's performance was a wipeout — they lost by 50 points." (A crushing defeat.)

The noun is used both for physical crashes and for complete defeats or destructions.
Tone and Register: When and Where Is This Phrase Used?

"Wipe out" is primarily an informal to semi-formal phrase. Here is a breakdown:

Very informal (casual conversation, sports talk):
Using it to mean exhaustion ("I'm wiped out") or a crash in sports ("He wiped out").

Informal to semi-formal (news, storytelling, everyday writing):
Using it to mean destruction or financial ruin ("The storm wiped out the crops").

Formal writing: You would likely avoid "wipe out" in highly formal or academic writing and prefer phrases like "eradicated," "eliminated," "devastated," or "obliterated" instead. However, it is not wrong to use "wipe out" even in moderately formal contexts.

"Wipe out" is a phrasal verb — a verb ("wipe") combined with a particle ("out") that together create a new meaning, different from "wipe" alone.

An important grammar point: this phrasal verb is separable, meaning the object can go between "wipe" and "out" or after "out."

Both of these are correct:

  • "The storm wiped out the village." ✅
  • "The storm wiped the village out." ✅

However, when you use a pronoun (him, her, it, them), it must go between "wipe" and "out":

  • "The storm wiped it out." ✅
  • "The storm wiped out it." ❌
Similar Phrases and How "Wipe Out" Differs

Understanding related phrases will sharpen your grasp of "wipe out."

"Wipe out" vs. "wipe off"
"Wipe off" means to clean something from a surface — "Wipe the stain off the table." It is literal and small in scale. "Wipe out" suggests total destruction on a much bigger scale.

"Wipe out" vs. "wear out"
"Wear out" also means to exhaust, but it usually implies a gradual process — "The long illness wore him out over months." "Wipe out" suggests exhaustion that happens more quickly and completely — "That one workout wiped me out."

"Wipe out" vs. "wipe away"
"Wipe away" is gentler — it means to gently remove something, often emotions or small things: "She wiped away her tears." "Wipe out" is stronger, more violent, and more complete.

"Wipe out" vs. "knock out"
"Knock out" can also mean to exhaust someone, but it also specifically means to make someone unconscious (in boxing or otherwise). "Wipe out" in the exhaustion sense is more about draining energy, not unconsciousness.
Real-Life Contexts Where You'll Hear "Wipe Out"

• Nature and disaster news: "The tsunami wiped out entire coastal towns."
  • War and history: "The army was wiped out in the battle."
  • Finance: "The crash wiped out her retirement fund."
  • Surfing/skateboarding culture: "Did you see that wipeout on the halfpipe?"
  • Daily life conversation: "I'm totally wiped out — I need to sleep."
  • Sports commentary: "That tackle completely wiped out the striker."
  • Biology/ecology: "Habitat loss wiped out several bird species in that region."

SituationWhat "wipe out" means

If you're talking about destruction — "wipe out" means to destroy completely. If you're talking about money — it means to lose everything. If you're talking about your energy — it means to feel completely drained. If you're talking about sports — it means to crash hard. If you're talking about crime or conflict — it means to kill or eliminate entirely.

The unifying thread across every single use: complete and total removal, with little or nothing left behind.

That is everything you need to know about "wipe out" — its meanings, grammar, tone, related phrases, and real-world usage. You now have the full picture.
17478: Think of a metal wire. It's thin. It's not big or heavy. But try to snap it — it's tough, stiff, and springy. Wiry borrows exactly these qualities and applies them to two things: a person's body, and the texture of hair (or fur).

When a person is described as wiry, it means they are lean and thin, but quietly strong and surprisingly tough.

A wiry person doesn't have large, bulging muscles. Their body is compact and light. But there's a hidden toughness inside that slender frame. They have strong endurance, good stamina, and a kind of "don't underestimate me" strength. Think of a long-distance runner, a rock climber, a jockey, or a seasoned farmer who has worked outdoors for decades. Small frame. No bulk. But built to last.

The key feeling of the word: lean + tough + strong in a quiet, efficient way.

How it differs from similar words:

  • Skinny = just thin, often implying weakness. No hidden strength.
  • Slim / slender = thin, but says nothing about toughness or strength.
  • Muscular / buff = visibly strong, often bulky and large.
  • Wiry = thin AND tough, with the strength packed inside that lean build — not on display.

This sense also applies to animals. A wiry little terrier or a wiry mountain goat is small and lean, but full of energy, toughness, and surprising strength.

Example sentences:

  • "He was a wiry young boxer — not big, but fast and incredibly hard to tire out."
  • "Despite her wiry frame, she hiked forty kilometers without complaint."
  • "The wiry old shepherd could outwork men half his age."

When hair, fur, a beard, or any similar material is described as wiry, it means it is stiff, coarse, rough, and springy — like actual wire. It doesn't feel soft, smooth, or silky. It has a bristly, almost scratchy quality, and it tends to stick out or resist lying flat.

Think of:

  • A dog's rough, bristly coat (terriers are famous for their wiry fur)
  • A coarse beard that scratches your cheek
  • Eyebrows that are thick, stiff, and impossible to tame with a brush
  • Hair that feels rough and snaps back into shape when you try to flatten it

How it differs from similar words:

  • Curly = describes the shape of the hair, not how it feels. Curly hair can still be soft.
  • Thick = describes the volume of hair. Wiry describes the texture — how it feels.
  • Coarse = the closest synonym for wiry hair. Wiry carries a bit more of that "springy and resistant" quality.
  • Soft / silky = the opposite of wiry.

Example sentences:

  • "The terrier had a wiry coat that felt like a scrubbing brush."
  • "He had a wiry beard that scratched her cheek whenever he hugged her."
  • "Her wiry curls bounced as she walked, refusing to be tamed by any comb."

Occasionally, in more literary or descriptive writing, wiry is used for a thin, high-pitched, metallic-sounding voice or noise — the kind of sound a plucked wire might make. This is rare, but worth knowing if you encounter it. Example: "He spoke in a wiry, strained voice."
Why both meanings feel like the same word

Both meanings trace back to the same visual idea: a metal wire is thin but tough (→ a wiry body) and stiff and resistant (→ wiry hair). Once you picture actual wire, the word clicks into place and stays there.

For a body: Usually admiring or at least respectful. It suggests someone is tough, resilient, and not to be underestimated. There's a sense of efficiency — no wasted bulk, just what works. It's often used for people who have earned their fitness through hard physical work or demanding sport, not through a gym.

For hair: Neutral to slightly negative. Wiry hair tends to be difficult to manage, rough to the touch, and hard to style.
What can be described as wiry

• People: a wiry old farmer, a wiry young athlete, a wiry teenager
  • Body parts: wiry arms, wiry legs (lean and strong)
  • Animals: a wiry little dog, a wiry racehorse, a wiry cat
  • Hair and fur: wiry hair, a wiry beard, wiry eyebrows, a wiry coat
  • Plants: wiry stems (thin, stiff, tough)
  • Grass: wiry grass (coarse, tough, low-growing grass, hard to pull out)

• a wiry build / wiry frame / wiry physique
  • a wiry little dog / a wiry old man
  • wiry hair / wiry curls / wiry beard
  • wiry stems / wiry grass

In one sentence: Wiry means lean and tough (for a body or animal) or stiff, coarse, and springy (for hair or fur) — always with the feeling of a wire: thin, but not weak.
17479:
Wisdom is the ability to consistently make good judgments, take right actions, and understand life deeply — not just by knowing facts, but by knowing what truly matters, how things really work, and what the right thing to do is in any given situation.

If you had to put it in a single sentence: wisdom is knowing what to do with what you know, and why.
Why Wisdom Is Special: What It Is Not

To really understand wisdom, you need to see how it's different from things that look similar.

Wisdom is not the same as intelligence.
An intelligent person thinks quickly, solves problems cleverly, and grasps complex ideas fast. But a person can be brilliant and still make terrible decisions — they can be selfish, short-sighted, or emotionally destructive. Intelligence is the power of the mind. Wisdom is knowing how to use that power well.

Wisdom is not the same as knowledge.
Knowledge is information you've learned. You can memorize an entire medical textbook and still have no idea how to comfort a dying patient or tell someone a hard truth with care. Knowledge gives you the what. Wisdom gives you the how, the when, and the why.

Wisdom is not the same as experience.
Many people live 80 years and repeat the same mistakes for 80 years. Experience is just what happens to you. Wisdom is what you learn from what happens to you — the lessons you extract, the patterns you notice, the understanding you build from pain, failure, success, and careful reflection.

Wisdom, in short, is the rare thing you get when knowledge, experience, reflection, and good judgment all come together.

Wisdom has several layers. Here's what it really consists of:

1. Deep Understanding
A wise person doesn't just know facts on the surface — they understand how things actually work. They see causes and effects, they understand human nature, they grasp why situations unfold the way they do. A wise doctor doesn't just know the medical facts; they understand what patients actually fear, what motivates people to change their habits, and what a family is really going through.

2. Good Judgment
This is perhaps the most visible sign of wisdom. A wise person consistently makes decisions that turn out to be right — not because they're lucky, but because they weigh things correctly. They know what matters and what doesn't. They can tell the difference between an urgent-looking problem that is minor and a quiet-looking problem that is serious.

3. Knowing What You Don't Know
One of the oldest ideas in philosophy is that wisdom begins with recognizing the limits of your own understanding. A wise person doesn't pretend to know more than they do. They are aware of their blind spots and biases. This intellectual humility is a mark of wisdom because overconfidence is one of the main roots of bad judgment.

4. Seeing the Bigger Picture
Wise people are not trapped in the moment. They can zoom out. When something feels urgent or terrible right now, a wise person can say: "In the grand scheme of things, how much will this matter?" They understand that many things pass, that many crises resolve, and that the choices we make in difficult moments define us.

5. Emotional Maturity
Wisdom includes the ability to manage your own emotions — to not act rashly when angry, to not crumble when afraid, to feel compassion for others even when it's inconvenient. A wise person doesn't let their feelings override their better judgment. They feel deeply, but they think clearly.

6. Knowing What Is Truly Good
Wisdom has a moral dimension. A clever person knows how to achieve goals. A wise person also knows which goals are worth having. They understand what a good life actually looks like — not just what feels good in the short term, but what is genuinely valuable over a lifetime. This is why wisdom is closely connected to ethics, to living well, and to caring about others.

Wisdom cannot be taught like a math formula. It grows slowly, through several things working together:

  • Experience gives you the raw material — the situations, the mistakes, the surprises of life.
  • Reflection is what turns experience into understanding. If you never stop to think about what happened and why, experience teaches you nothing.
  • Learning from others — listening to people wiser than yourself, reading deeply, being open to correction — accelerates the process.
  • Failure and suffering, handled thoughtfully, are some of the greatest teachers of wisdom. Almost every genuinely wise person has gone through significant hardship and chosen to learn from it rather than harden from it.

This is why wisdom is so often associated with age and older people. Time gives you more chances to experience, fail, reflect, and correct course. But age alone doesn't create wisdom — there are foolish old people and wise young people. The difference is always whether a person has genuinely reflected on their life and genuinely tried to understand it.

Wisdom shows up not in grand dramatic moments, but constantly, in small choices:

  • A wise parent knows when to give a child the answer to a problem and when to let the child struggle and figure it out themselves.
  • A wise friend knows when to offer advice and when to simply listen.
  • A wise worker knows when to push back on a bad idea and when to stay quiet and pick their battles.
  • A wise person in an argument knows when they might actually be wrong, and has the courage to admit it.
  • A wise person facing tragedy knows how to grieve without being permanently destroyed by it.

In every case, wisdom is not about having more information — it's about applying what you know, at the right time, in the right way, for the right reasons.

The word "wisdom" is also used to describe the accumulated understanding of a group, culture, or tradition over a long time. When we say the "wisdom of the ancients" or "traditional wisdom," we mean the practical knowledge and insights that generations of humans have gathered through centuries of living, struggling, and observing. Proverbs, philosophical teachings, religious texts, and cultural traditions often carry this kind of wisdom — compressed lessons that entire civilizations learned the hard way.

The phrase "words of wisdom" means advice or insight that reflects deep understanding — something worth taking seriously, not just a surface-level opinion.

"Conventional wisdom" means beliefs that most people in a society accept as true or standard. Interestingly, conventional wisdom is not always actually wise — it's sometimes just widely shared habit or assumption.

"Pearls of wisdom" are small but precious pieces of insight — a single powerful idea that opens your eyes.
A Final Way to Think About It

Imagine three people facing a difficult, morally complicated situation — say, a friend has made a mistake and is about to face serious consequences.

  • The knowledgeable person can explain exactly what the rules say and what will happen.
  • The intelligent person can quickly analyze the situation and come up with clever options.
  • The wise person knows what the right thing to do is — they weigh their loyalty to the friend, the fairness owed to others affected, the long-term consequences, the friend's own growth, and the kind of person they themselves want to be. And then they act in a way that is genuinely good — not just convenient, not just clever, but right.

That is wisdom: the capacity to do what is truly good, guided by deep understanding, good judgment, and the humility to know your own limits.
